atoms.canonical_statement: The study proposes NeSy-RAG, a modular neuro-symbolic RAG framework intended to provide explainable question answering with source-attributable symbolic reasoning and explicit detection of missing user context.
NeSy-RAG is designed as a plug-in extension to an existing RAG system and takes the retrieved text chunks and the user question as inputs to a symbolic reasoning pipeline.
For each retrieved text chunk, NeSy-RAG synthesizes a separate Prolog module containing rules and facts derived from that chunk.
The modular Prolog representation allows every synthesized rule and fact used in reasoning to be uniquely mapped back to its originating text chunk.
The framework assumes Boolean user questions accompanied by user-specific contextual information that may be incomplete and therefore may require follow-up questions.
During Prolog synthesis, facts are separated into universal facts and dynamic facts; a dynamic fact has at least one argument whose value cannot be determined from domain knowledge at synthesis time.
The prototype focuses on dynamic facts with a single Boolean argument, although the authors state that the approach could be extended to more complex data types and argument structures.

When a dynamic predicate is evaluated, an interaction method requests or validates the missing Boolean value, asserts the acquired value in Prolog, and returns that Boolean result to the predicate evaluation.
NeSy-RAG formulates query construction as selection and composition of available predicates rather than asking the LLM to inspect the complete knowledge base to determine bindings.
During module synthesis, the system creates 0-arity rules that expose module functionality as self-contained Boolean claims.
At inference time, extracted 0-arity rules are ranked against the user question by cosine similarity using a joint natural-language–programming-language embedding model.
The query-generating LLM is constrained to compose a Prolog query only from the most relevant retrieved 0-arity rules.
NeSy-RAG uses hierarchical retrieval in two stages: first retrieving question-relevant text chunks and then retrieving question-relevant 0-arity predicates from the corresponding modules.
Executing the generated Prolog query yields a symbolic response and an execution trace whose rules and facts retain module and source-chunk attribution for later verification.
The evaluation uses ShARC, a conversational question-answering benchmark built from UK government legal text, with target labels yes, no, irrelevant, or more.
The reported evaluation uses the ShARC test split containing 8,276 entries.

The scenario, evidence, and prior interaction history for each ShARC instance are consolidated into a context field that is withheld initially, and a separate LLM simulates an ideal user by answering system follow-up questions from that context.
To simulate retrieval, each target snippet is presented together with randomly sampled distractor snippets from the ShARC test split.
Because each ShARC instance relies on a single relevant snippet, multi-hop retrieval is outside the scope of the reported evaluation.
The prototype independently classifies each candidate snippet as relevant or irrelevant and predicts irrelevant if no snippet is classified as relevant.
Synthesized Prolog modules are reusable across future questions, so module synthesis need not be repeated for every question over the same snippet.
If the query-generation LLM returns None because no suitable query can be constructed from the retrieved predicates, the prototype predicts irrelevant.

If the simulated user cannot answer a necessary dynamic predicate, the prototype evaluates the query under both Boolean assignments; it predicts more if the outcome changes and otherwise returns the consistent yes or no result.
The prototype caches evaluated dynamic predicates and their answers during a conversation to avoid asking identical follow-up questions repeatedly.
The LLM Upper Baseline receives the singular target snippet, the question, and the complete user context and directly predicts the target label without generating follow-up questions.

The LLM RAG Baseline selects relevant snippets, predicts an answer without initial user context, generates follow-up questions when the initial prediction is more, and then predicts the final label after receiving the simulated answers.

exposures.details: pure LLM inference with follow-up-question generation

atoms.canonical_statement: The experiments use gpt-oss:20b and gpt-5-mini for LLM calls, jina-code-embeddings-1.5b for 0-arity predicate embedding and retrieval, and run gpt-oss:20b through Ollama on an NVIDIA RTX 3090.
The synthetic retrieval set contains three snippets per instance, including the instance snippet.

The number of retrieved snippets was not varied in the evaluation; the authors state that independent per-snippet relevance filtering makes an accuracy effect unlikely, but this expectation was not tested.
The LLM RAG Baseline using gpt-oss:20b achieved 42.8% accuracy on ShARC.
The LLM RAG Baseline using gpt-oss:20b had an average execution duration of 11.4 seconds per ShARC instance.

outcome.measurement_method: Mean processing time per dataset instance, seconds

atoms.canonical_statement: The trained BiAE reference result reported in Table 2 is 77.9% accuracy on ShARC.
There were 178 NeSy-RAG execution errors, corresponding to 2.2% of the 8,276 ShARC test instances, caused by syntactically invalid Prolog modules or queries.

outcome.measurement_method: Executions failing because of syntactically invalid Prolog modules or queries

atoms.canonical_statement: For gold-label more instances, NeSy-RAG correctly classified 61%, compared with 19% for the LLM RAG baseline and 23% for the LLM Upper baseline.

atoms.canonical_statement: NeSy-RAG misclassified 31% of gold-label yes instances as more, the dominant reported NeSy-RAG error pattern.
Among gold-label more instances, NeSy-RAG misclassified 17% as yes and 15% as no.
The authors conclude that NeSy-RAG can outperform a standard same-model LLM RAG baseline in both ShARC accuracy and mean execution time while using symbolic reasoning.

The authors attribute NeSy-RAG’s lower mean execution time to reusable per-snippet Prolog modules, query construction over a small retrieved predicate set, and algorithmic triggering of follow-up questions without an extra LLM generation call.
A systematic evaluation of token savings relative to standard LLM-based pipelines was not performed.
Whether NeSy-RAG benefits from a larger language model was not evaluated.

The primary remaining error identified by the authors is over-generation of dynamic predicates, which can trigger unnecessary follow-up questions and cause answerable yes instances to be classified as more.
The authors characterize NeSy-RAG’s tendency to return more instead of a definitive answer as a conservative bias that may be preferable to false certainty in high-stakes domains.
Despite its conservative bias, NeSy-RAG still produced false-certain answers for some gold-label more instances.
The reported knowledge-gap mechanism is limited to Boolean dynamic predicates; broader data types and argument structures remain future work.
NeSy-RAG’s overall performance is contingent on the quality of the underlying retrieval mechanism and the available domain knowledge.
Extending the evaluation to multi-hop and multi-chunk reasoning is identified as future work.

The Prolog-generation prompt requires user-provided facts to be dynamic arity-1 predicates with a single true/false argument, to represent only the minimum necessary user information, and to be separated from derived knowledge.
The Prolog-generation prompt instructs the model to encode rules for legal outcomes and to add the corresponding negated scenarios.
The 0-arity-rule generation prompt instructs the model to create 0-arity rules that act as question-answering interfaces to non-0-arity rules in the synthesized knowledge base.
The query-generation prompt requires the generated Prolog query to use only the supplied 0-arity predicates and to include module names for the predicates used.
